details:
Outpost Command is a browser game for children aged 7 to 12. The player is the Junior Flight Director of a three-astronaut crew on the Moon or Mars for seven days. They balance power, life support, and radiation shielding, and manage the crew’s science. Real NASA space-weather data from DONKI shapes the game. The title screen shows the latest saved solar flare record, and where that record is available, its class sets the speed of the Flare Wave mini-game, where children tap flares to protect the habitat dome with their hands. Every choice has a cost, so no option is free. After each mission, a Learning Report shows what changed and why, with links to NASA sources.

How it works: The game runs in any browser with no download or account. Gameplay is deterministic, so the same settings always produce the same events. The Day 1 guided tutorial shows one control at a time, and a character called Bolt reads instructions aloud.

Impact: Teachers can run the game in class with a class code and a printable discussion sheet. Children learn engineering trade-offs through play. There are no ads, no accounts, and no tracking, and all progress stays on the child’s device.

Tools and technologies: Vite, React 18, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Framer Motion, the Web Speech API for read-aloud, WebAudio for sound, and vitest for tests. Hosted on Vercel.

Creativity: Outpost Command combines a survival game with hands-on play. Real space-weather events set the flares, and a tap-based Flare Wave turns a balancing decision into an action children can feel.

Factors considered: Ages 7 to 12 with a guardian present, plain language at Grade 2 to 4 reading level, reduced-motion and keyboard support, large tap targets, offline play, and no tracking or dark patterns.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) (paste into the SI question, or describe in the box that asks where and how SI was used)

We used GitHub Copilot (agent mode in Visual Studio Code) to generate much of the code for the screens, components, and engine interfaces, based on written prompts. The team kept an AI usage log listing each prompt, what the AI generated, and what a human reviewed or changed. A human reviewed and tested all AI-generated code, and the game’s balance values, science sources, and child-facing text were reviewed by the team. No AI-generated images or video are used. Code and data generated with SI are acknowledged here and in the repository’s AI usage log.

Before you paste the SI answer, confirm the AI-generated share from your log, since judges will look for an honest description. Send me the video link and playtest notes when you have them, and I’ll add them to the form text.
